pulls.title: wallet: return broadcast errors from CommitTransaction
pulls.body:
Part of https://github.com/bitcoin-core/gui-qml/issues/1008.

The QML GUI shows "Transaction sent" even when the node rejected the transaction, because `CWallet::CommitTransaction()` only logs the rejection and returns `void`. 
This PR bubbles up the submission result through `interfaces::Wallet::commitTransaction()` so the GUI can report it.

#### Key changes
- Introduce `TransactionBroadcastError`, holding a `TransactionError` code and an untranslated message.
- Commit/Broadcast functions returns `Expected<void, TransactionBroadcastError>`. 
  - Remove `TransactionError::OK`, a success value in an error enum.
- Add a `SUBMISSION_SKIPPED` code for when the wallet doesn't submit the transaction (broadcasting disabled, abandoned, coinbase, confirmed or conflicted). `SubmitTxMemoryPoolAndRelay()` previously returned `false` in these cases.

#### Note
- Existing callers (wallet RPCs, Qt widgets, fee bumper) ignore the new result, so their behavior and RPC responses don't change.
- `commitBumpTransaction()` similarly reports success for a rejected replacement. This will be addressed in a follow-up PR.
- gui-qml will need to update its `interfaces::Wallet` mock for the new `commitTransaction()` signature.

pulls.title: net: make orphan reconsideration more granular
pulls.body:
We currently concentrate the validation of all the assigned peer’s reconsiderable orphans that are still missing inputs in a single message-processing turn. This ties orphan processing to validation result, and adds latency to processing other peers' messages.

Always process a single reconsiderable orphan per turn instead. This removes the need for an immediate validation result, and shifts the latency from other peers to the assigned peer.

pulls.title: rpc: add testsubmitpackage for 1p1c test submissions
pulls.body:
A test-only companion to submitpackage that validates a strict 1p1c [parent, child] bundle without mutating the mempool. Intended as a wallet pre-flight check for CPFP fee-bumping packages.

Enables rbf and sibling eviction evaluation, just like submitpackage.

Diverging behaviors from submitpackage:

Hard rejects packages that aren't exactly 2 txs in a child-with-parents topology, and parents that pass individual acceptance (caller should use testsubmitpackage on parent alone for that).

---

To do this "properly" without rejecting the self-sufficient parents (and not giving surprising results that don't match reality), we would need fairly extensive changes to mempool acceptance logic, more book-keeping to unroll test-accepted subpackage state (while risking mutating the mempool in brittle ways), and possibly other changes.

This is a partial addressing of https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/32160, hopefully addressing most of the missing functionality people are requesting.

pulls.title: net: limit relative ban times to uint32
pulls.body:
`BanMan::Ban` computes the ban end as `GetTime() + bantime` (banman.cpp:140). `setban` and `-bantime` both accept any int64, so a relative bantime close to `INT64_MAX`:

```
setban 1.2.3.5 add 9223372036854775807
```

returns success, but the sum overflows. UBSan reports:

```
src/banman.cpp:140:73: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 1790412558 + 9223372036854775807 cannot be represented in type 'int64_t'
```

Without UBSan the result wraps negative, the ban is treated as already expired, and it is silently dropped. With `-bantime=9223372036854775807` the same happens to every `setban add` that uses the default duration.

This limits relative ban times to uint32 (about 136 years):

- `setban` rejects a relative bantime above `UINT32_MAX` with "Error: bantime is too large"
- `-bantime` is parsed as `uint32_t`, so larger values saturate at `UINT32_MAX`

Absolute timestamps are unchanged.

The added cases in `rpc_setban.py` check that `UINT32_MAX + 1` and `INT64_MAX` are rejected, that `UINT32_MAX` is accepted, and that with `-bantime=INT64_MAX` a default-duration ban is listed with a duration of `UINT32_MAX`. Both parts fail on master and pass with the change. `p2p_disconnect_ban.py` still passes.

AI tools were used to help find this issue and to prepare the patch and test.

pulls.title: wallet: harden external signer psbt processing, revamp mock
pulls.body:
The current external signer functional test mock can only echo a prepared PSBT. This gets in the way of testing more complicated scenarios, i.e. misbehaving signers and (MuSig2) multisig.

- *test: have external signer mock use a wallet*: gives the mock its own offline node and wallet with private keys, while the test uses the watch-only version.
- *external_signer: require matching PSBT versions*
- *external_signer: merge PSBT response instead of replacing*: tests signers that drop outputs, reduce their value or change the script. Merging rejects these changes while allowing signers to omit unnecessary PSBT fields.
- *external_signer: reject unsafe sighash types*
- *external_signer: **reject finalized PSBT inputs***: keeps the above check simple. Documents this new requirement. HWI does not finalize.

The remaining commits prepare the test helpers and enforce IWYU for `src/external_signer.cpp`.

This PR absorbs the scenarios from #35358, but is better able to test them thanks to the new mock signer implementation.

This PR does not intend to fully harden against a malicious external signer, and can't protect against a malicious HWI (equivalent) process running as the same user.

pulls.title: test: deduplicate PSBT unknown-field coverage in `rpc_psbt.py`
pulls.body:
I've tested some mutations related to test coverage for PSBT unknown field merging and discovered an inconsistency.
<details>

If line 71 of `psbt.cpp` "`unknown.insert(psbt.unknown.begin(), psbt.unknown.end());`"  (inside `bool PartiallySignedTransaction::Merge(const PartiallySignedTransaction& psbt)` function) is removed then, the expected test fails: *"Test that combining PSBTs preserves unknown fields with the same and with distinct values per map."*

If line 434 of `psbt.cpp` "`unknown.insert(input.unknown.begin(), input.unknown.end());`" (inside `bool PSBTInput::Merge(const PSBTInput& input)` function), is removed, a different unexpected test fails: "*Test that unknown values are just passed through*".

If line 537 of `psbt.cpp` "`unknown.insert(output.unknown.begin(), output.unknown.end());`" (inside `bool PSBTOutput::Merge(const PSBTOutput& output)` function), is removed, the expected test fails: "*Test that combining PSBTs preserves unknown fields with the same and with distinct values per map.*".
</details>

This PR solves this inconsistency.
The old code did 3 different things:
1. Test the pass-through of unknown values for `walletprocesspsbt`.
2. Combine two v0 PSBTs with different unknown input keys and check that both keys survive.
3. Combine implicit v0 PSBT with explicit v0 and check that both keys survive.

Case 2 is already fully covered by the existing `test_combinepsbt_preseves_unknown_fields` so keeping it is redundant and misleading.

Commit 40eba5eb20ba0041a6328ba3482fcc26ddbe0185 moves the old code into a new method called `test_unknown_fields_passthrough` and commit ef4310097bd651497a98a9d1bb59560a7055ae01 removes the redundant code of Case 2 and moves Case 3 inside `test_combinepsbt_preserves_unknown_fields`.

The proxy option also maintains its own network-name mapping while `-onlynet` and `getnodeaddresses` use the shared parser.

pulls.title: [32.x] Backports
net: require a dedicated bind for automatic Tor
pulls.body:
**Problem:** When the automatic onion service has no dedicated `-bind=<addr>=onion`, Tor forwards incoming connections to the first normal P2P bind. A wildcard onion bind also fails to identify incoming Tor connections. In either case, network classification is incorrect and Tor peers may inherit permissions granted to the Tor daemon's IP address.

**Fix:** Refuse startup when `-listenonion` is enabled and an explicit `-bind` configuration lacks a dedicated, non-wildcard onion bind or includes a wildcard onion bind, following [the recommendation in #34892](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34892#issuecomment-5541662236). Users should add a specific `-bind=<addr>=onion` or set `-listenonion=0`.

Because `-listenonion` is enabled by default when listening, existing configurations with only a normal `-bind` must also be updated. Nodes without explicit `-bind` options retain the default dedicated onion listener.

pulls.title: rpc: flag invalid taproot leaf control blocks in decodepsbt
pulls.body:
`decodepsbt` shows each `PSBT_IN_TAP_LEAF_SCRIPT` record as-is. It does
not say whether its control block could be a genuine leaf of the input's
taproot tree. `InferTaprootTree()` already checks this, but silently
skips whatever fails. That is correct there: one bad candidate among
several script paths is not an error. But it means a PSBT with an
unusable leaf shows no sign of it.

This PR adds a diagnostic only; signing does not change. A new optional
`control_block_warnings` array, next to `control_blocks`, gives the first
check a control block fails. There are four checks:

- leaf version (must be even);
- control block size;
- leaf-version byte (must match `leaf_ver`);
- Merkle root (must match `PSBT_IN_TAP_MERKLE_ROOT`).

The Merkle-root check needs `PSBT_IN_TAP_MERKLE_ROOT`, which is optional
per BIP371. When it is absent, only the other three checks run, and the
help text says so.

Similar in spirit to #25513, which added the same kind of check for
`PSBT_OUT_TAP_TREE`.

## Commits

1. Unit test for the four checks in `InferTaprootTree()` (none existed).
2. Extract the checks into `CheckTapLeafCandidate()`, shared by
   `InferTaprootTree()` and `decodepsbt`.
3. `decodepsbt`'s new `control_block_warnings` field, with its
   functional test.

*Made with my usual tools: a computer, the Internet and an LLM. The mistakes, as usual, are all mine.*

pulls.title: compressor: oversized script decoding can leave a spendable script
pulls.body:
**Problem:** The oversized-script fallback appends `OP_RETURN` to the destination instead of replacing it. If the destination already contains an unfinished push, the appended byte becomes pushed data and the result can remain spendable.

**Fix:** Replace the destination with `OP_RETURN` rather than appending it.

Found while reviewing #36280. This predates that PR and appears latent because oversized outputs are excluded from the UTXO set, but it could affect malformed stored records decoded into a reused destination.

pulls.title: headersync: do parameter search at runtime
pulls.body:
This migrates the headers presync parameters (`commitment_period` and `redownload_buffer_size`) from being precomputed chainparams to being computed at runtime whenever a headers sync starts. This has as advantages:
* Less work for maintainers that need to occasionally run the current `contrib/devtools/headerssync-params.py` script.
* Less room for mistakes in that process.
* Automatically adapts based on time (as opposed to needing to predict the lifetime of the software).

To achieve this, the parameter search algorithm is implemented in C++. It is simpler, because it does not attempt to model the fact that the attacker is forced to submit their headers in batches of 2000 if they want to maintain the attack. The old Python code did that, but actually got it (slightly) wrong by missing the fact that attackers are capable of strategically deciding to stop the attack in the middle of a batch (found by darosior).

Unit tests and fuzz tests are added, and at the end the old Python code is deleted.

pulls.title: Test: Add P2SH scriptSig stack-size boundary tests
pulls.body:
VerifyScript runs a P2SH scriptPubKey on the stack the scriptSig leaves before handling the redeemScript. The 20-byte push in HASH160 <20> EQUAL adds one item, so a scriptSig that leaves 1,000 items fails with STACK_SIZE, while 999 items is valid.

An implementation that checks the redeemScript hash without running the scriptPubKey accepts the 1,000-item spend. No existing vector leaves the scriptSig at this boundary, so such an implementation can pass every row.

Add 999 and 1,000 item cases with P2SH and WITNESS, and the 1,000 item case with no flags, which fails the same way because the scriptPubKey always runs. Also add the same boundary during redeemScript evaluation, where the restored stack plus the redeemScript's pushes reach 1,000 and 1,001 items.

The same case is added as a feature_taproot spender in #36455, so its dump can be added to the script assets (bitcoin-core/qa-assets#297).

These were discovered by finding gaps in an alternate implementation (rbitcoin)

pulls.title: wallet: only rebroadcast transactions originating from the wallet
pulls.body:
As explained in #3828, rebroadcast of transactions paying the wallet (but not spending any wallet inputs) is a privacy leak, since anyone can generate these, choose a low fee, and observe who rebroadcasts them. 
While it is somewhat intuitive that submitting transactions has privacy implications - at least until confirmation - this is manageable by various strategies (switching to privacy networks for a while, using private broadcast, making sure it confirms before rebroadcast). However, I find it rather unexpected that just passively running a node with a wallet loaded can lead to a loss of privacy as well.

This PR stops rebroadcasting transactions that don't spend any wallet inputs. For the same reason, they are also no longer re-added to the mempool on startup or after an import: otherwise our node might be the only one still having a transaction the rest of the network has dropped, which can be detected with active probing (e.g. by submitting a child).

This does have the trade-off that receivers (who have an incentive to get paid) will now need to manually resubmit transactions if the transaction doesn't confirm and the sender doesn't rebroadcast, but I think it is worth the privacy benefit.

An alternative approach is https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36380, although these could also be combined (make rebroadcast optional, but never rebroadcast non-originating transactions)

Fixes #3828

pulls.title: test: add tests in script test suites covering script.cpp live mutants
pulls.body:
Add direct unit tests in `script_tests`, `sigopcount_tests`, `script_standard_tests`, and `script_segwit_tests` covering edge cases in `src/script/script.cpp`.

These tests cover strict 34-byte Taproot script recognition and non-minimal pushdata rejection (killing surviving mutant 2347 from mutation run 21), outer `scriptSig` opcode parsing for `OP_16` and `OP_NOP` in `CScript::GetSigOpCount`, single-byte mismatches against the 2-byte anchor payload `{0x4e, 0x73}`, truncated length field handling in `GetScriptOp` for `OP_PUSHDATA4` (killing surviving mutant 2383), `MAX_OPCODE` boundary checks in `HasValidOps` (killing surviving mutant 2365), and delimiter formatting for single-element witness stacks in `CScriptWitness::ToString` (killing surviving mutant 2362).

pulls.title: wallet: Only broadcast resubmitted transactions that were added to the mempool
pulls.body:
As discussed in #36403, one of the issues with current rebroadcast behavior is that the rebroadcast begins an unconditional relay of a transaction to peers. While this is broadcast is limited to peers that have not previously been inv'd the transaction, there is still a privacy leak in this double relay of a transaction, especially so for transactions that are still in nodes' mempools.

This PR changes the rebroadcast to only rebroadcast transactions if the transaction was not already present in our mempool. This provides some additional privacy while retaining intended rebroadcast behavior as transactions that have likely fallen out of nodes' mempools are the ones that actually need to be rebroadcast.

The wallet rebroadcast tests are additionally refactored for isolation so that their behaviors can still be tested after this change. Additionally, a test for the loading resubmission was added, as well as a test for the new behavior.

pulls.title: descriptor: Represent multipath descriptors in a single Descriptor object
pulls.body:
Currently, multipath descriptor strings treat the multipath specifiers as syntactic sugar. Once we finish parsing such a string, the multipath elements are lost as the result is the multiple distinct descriptors that the multipath is a shorthand for. This means that we are unable to return the multipath string for such descriptors.

This PR allows descriptors to actually be multipath where the multipath specifiers are represented inside of the paths of `BIP32PubkeyProvider`s. This allows for the multipath string to be produced.

In order to achieve this, a lot of derivation path parsing is refactored. `KeyPath` is promoted to being its own class (which subclasses `std::vector`), while the individual derivation indexes become a `KeyPathElement` object so that the multipath elements can be represented. Furthermore, hardened derivation characters are now being stored within `KeyPathElement`s so each element knows what the original hardened character was. This also cleans up a little bit of the descriptor implementation as we no longer have to carry around `bool apostrophe` in a bunch of places.

Lastly, `Parse` now returns a single `Descriptor` object, rather than a vector of them. If the descriptor is a multipath descriptor, the expansion can be retrieved using `GetMultipathExpansion()`. The wallet uses this and still must not store multipath descriptors.

pulls.body:
#36442 allows multipath descriptors to be represented in a single `Descriptor` object. `GetMultipathExpansion` returns the multiple descriptors represented by a multipath descriptor. This expansion is reversible - given the expansion in the order of the multipath elements, it is possible to determine what the original multipath descriptor was. pulls.title: private broadcast: wait synchronously for mempool acceptance
pulls.body:
Calling `BroadcastTransaction` with the `NO_MEMPOOL_PRIVATE_BROADCAST` method skips inserting the transaction into the mempool and returns immediately. This causes problems with software that expects the transaction to be in the mempool after the function returns. For example many third-party wallets or services call `sendrawtransaction` and expect the transaction to be in the mempool after it returns a successful response.

This PR adds a new `TransactionAddedToMempoolSync` method to `CValidationInterface`. This is then used in `BroadcastTransaction` when the method is `NO_MEMPOOL_PRIVATE_BROADCAST` to wait for the transaction to have been accepted back into the mempool before returning. It also adds a timeout (default 10 minutes) to `BroadcastTransaction` and exposes it as an option for `sendrawtransaction`. Setting the timeout to 0 disables the wait and returns immediately, preserving the current behavior.

Synchronously waiting for mempool acceptance is also a prerequisite for adding private broadcast support to the wallet. The `TransactionAddedToMempoolSync` method is added specifically for future wallet broadcasting, so a broadcast caller holding `cs_wallet` will not timeout waiting on another background event that is also trying to acquire `cs_wallet`.

pulls.title: Implement BIP 54 (Consensus Cleanup) without mainnet activation
pulls.body:
This implements the Consensus Cleanup validation rules proposed in [BIP 54](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0054.md). These rules are only enabled on regtest. Mainnet activation, if any, is to be considered separately.

This patchset is based on the code that was previously reviewed ([1](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/99), [2](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/110)) and tested (for instance [here](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/consensus-cleanup-demo-of-slow-blocks-on-signet/2367)) on Bitcoin Inquisition. The tests and documentation have since been improved, but the consensus-critical commits have been carried over with only minor differences (the only behavioural one being the addition of the stripped-size check to `PreChecks`).

Roughly 95% of the added lines are tests or test data. The format, contents, and reproduction procedure for the BIP 54 test vectors are documented [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/tree/master/bip-0054/test_vectors). The `bip54_tests` unit test module exercises each mitigation extensively in isolation. The `feature_bip54.py` functional test verifies all of them end-to-end after and prior to activation. For the timestamp rules, it simulates timewarp and Murch–Zawy attacks, demonstrating the new timestamp rules prevent these exploits. A fuzz harness for the sigop accounting logic is also included, which can be seeded from the BIP test vectors (implemented [here](https://github.com/darosior/bitcoin/tree/bip54_seed_fuzz_corpus)).

See commit messages for details.

pulls.title: [wip,nomerge,rfc] build: Require C++23 compiler
pulls.body:
C++23 for Bitcoin Core is mostly a "style update" on top of C++20. However, the workarounds to avoid C++23 keep accumulating and some parts of the code already use C++23 features, such as lambda attributes (https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/commit/bdd0cd69418d189f62699d274a751cbf6d36bb43).

I don't know when it is fine to switch, but at some point, I think it is fine to require a C++23 compiler, so that [new stuff](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/34979#issuecomment-4448399166) is unlocked. Of course this requires bumping the minimum required compiler versions:

* GCC: 13
* Clang: 19

There are some C++23 features that aren't implemented (such as `<stacktrace>` not really shipped in any vanilla stdlib today), or e.g. `ranges::starts_with` not implemented until libstdc++-16. But overall I think we are better off using C++23 without those few features instead of waiting longer?

pulls.title: net: validate Tor onion service replies and cached keys
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A node creates its onion service through Tor's control protocol and caches the returned `PrivateKey` value for reconnects.
Tor reply parsing unescapes quoted values, so a control endpoint can return a value containing a line break or space.
On reconnect, the node inserts that value unquoted into an `ADD_ONION` command.
CRLF frames the remainder as a separate command, while a space adds further arguments.
An unprivileged local process can exploit this by impersonating the default loopback endpoint while Tor is unavailable, seeding the cache, and releasing the port before Tor is available again.
A compromised operator-configured endpoint can return the same malicious value.
The reply handler also continues after receiving an invalid service ID, logging it and caching the key before attempting to advertise the invalid address.
A later reply without a service ID can reuse an ID left by an earlier reply.

**Fix:** This PR validates the returned service ID as a Tor v3 onion address before logging it, caching the key, or advertising the service.
Each reply must provide its own service ID, and reply fields stay local until validation succeeds.
Key validation accepts `NEW:ED25519-V3` or an `ED25519-V3` key whose Base64 payload decodes to 64 bytes.
Returned keys are validated before adoption or caching, and cached keys are validated before reuse.
A malformed cached key leaves the onion service unavailable until the operator removes the file and restarts the node. It cannot inject another command or argument.

pulls.title: torcontrol: escape backslashes in -torpassword
pulls.body:
With `HASHEDPASSWORD` authentication, `TorController::protocolinfo_cb` sends the password as a quoted string, `AUTHENTICATE "<password>"` (torcontrol.cpp:667). It escapes `"` but not `\`.

Tor parses that argument as a control-spec QuotedString, where a backslash escapes the next character. So:

- `-torpassword=pa\ss` reaches Tor as `pass`, authentication fails and no onion service is created
- `-torpassword=pass\` escapes the closing quote, so the command is malformed

This escapes backslashes before quotes.

The new `test_password_escaping` in `feature_torcontrol.py` uses the mock control server with `HASHEDPASSWORD` and `-torpassword=pa\ss"word\`, and checks the exact `AUTHENTICATE` line. On master it gets `AUTHENTICATE "pa\ss\"word\"`, with the fix `AUTHENTICATE "pa\\ss\"word\\"`.

Tested against Tor 0.4.9.12 with `HashedControlPassword` set for `pa\ss"word\`: on master bitcoind logs "tor: Authentication failed", with this change authentication succeeds and ADD_ONION creates the onion service.

AI tools were used to help find this issue and to prepare the patch and test.

pulls.title: bloom: avoid undefined sizing calculations
pulls.body:
**Problem:** The four-argument `CBloomFilter` constructor is used by unit tests and the fuzz target to exercise Bloom filter sizing directly.
Zero elements make the hash-function calculation divide by zero.
The size calculation converts its floating-point result to `unsigned int` before applying the protocol limit, which is undefined for zero or invalid false-positive rates and for valid parameters whose calculated size exceeds the integer range.

**Fix:** Require false-positive rates in `[0, 1]`, construct the existing empty match-all state for zero elements, and use the largest permitted filter for a zero rate with positive elements.
Clamp the calculated size before its integer conversion so large valid inputs remain within the protocol limit.

pulls.title: CI: silent merge check
pulls.body:
In this design there is a new GHA job merged into the main repo that adds check runs to each PR on whether they have a silent merge conflict or not.

The idea is that we have a job that pretty much runs 24/7 triggered every 6 hours or so and set to run for 5.5 hours, it could be set to run on a GHA runner rather than a Cirrus runner. Obviously running on a Cirrus runner (or even multiple runners) would dramatically speed up how many PRs can be checked for silent merge conflicts.

The job uses the Github checks API to add a passing or failing test run to each PR directly. The silent merge check job itself should always pass, it writes pass or fail checks to the PRs.

It will look through all open PRs and discard anything that has a git merge failure or a failing test with the thinking that there is no point checking something that can't be merged anyway. Then it will select PRs that have not had a silent merge check and one by one pull the merge branch of the PR and the full CI job "Previous releases" on that branch.

When all PRs have been checked it will then re-check a PR that was checked the longest time ago.

pulls.title: test: cover unsatisfiable mining timestamp
pulls.body:
This PR adds test coverage for what happens in the (extremely unlikely) event that the miner can't satisfy the constraints. This is inspired by the recently added timewarp-protection and Murch-Zawy rules (for the miner, not for consensus, see #30681 and #35949), but this is a pre-existing issue. It is not made worse by these rules.

The test has an attacker mine 6 blocks, which set MTP at the victim's future-time limit. It calls `getblocktemplate` and the equivalent IPC method, which both fail. It then moves mock time one second forward, and demonstrates mining works again (and we don't drop the IPC connection).

This (impractical) attack can be done at any height, be we illustrate it for blocks 142, 143 and 0 of a retarget period, to clarify that the timewarp-protection and Murch-Zawy rules do not matter.

The test was added to `ipc_mining.py`, to avoid having to add IPC support to `mining_basic.py`. Mining coverage is currently split between various test files and not always mirrored between RPC and IPC. A followup could unify these, while still skipping the IPC side when that's not compiled.

A few refactor commits to prepare:

- fix incorrect name: `REGTEST_RETARGET_PERIOD` -> `HALVING_INTERVAL`
- drop `REGTEST_` prefix from `REGTEST_N_BITS` and `REGTEST_TARGET` (consistent with `HALVING_INTERVAL`, `DIFFICULTY_ADJUSTMENT_INTERVAL` and `TIME_GENESIS_BLOCK`).
- move `DIFFICULTY_ADJUSTMENT_INTERVAL` to the framework

pulls.title: kernel: make btck_LogEntry opaque
pulls.body:
Makes `btck_LogEntry` an opaque type with `btck_log_entry_get_*` accessors, instead of a public struct. This allows adding or changing fields without breaking the ABI, and is consistent with ~all other kernel objects. Follow-up to https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34374#discussion_r4207440088. 

I added a benchmark in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/compare/master...stickies-v:bitcoin:2026-10/kernel-logentry-bench, and found that performance is not meaningfully impacted either way. Some results below.

<details>
<summary>Performance stats</summary>

### Performance

Fields are now converted only when read, at the cost of a library call per field. The [benchmark](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/compare/master...stickies-v:bitcoin:2026-10/kernel-logentry-bench) measures a kernel log statement up to and including the callback (Apple M4 Pro, static library, `-O2`, median of 2×25 interleaved runs):

| Callback reads | master | PR | Delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| no fields | 57.4 ns | 55.2 ns | −1.6 to −2.5 ns |
| message only | 57.8 ns | 56.0 ns | −1.4 to −2.0 ns |
| all 9 fields | 57.9 ns | 62.7 ns | +4.8 to +5.4 ns |

Break-even is at 2-3 fields. Either way, the difference is small next to the ~50 ns the log statement costs before the callback, and to what a consumer typically does with the entry (formatting, I/O).
</details>

btcsignals: destroy callbacks on disconnect
pulls.body:
Currently callback functions connected to signals do not get freed when their `connection::disconnect` method is called or when their associated `scoped_connection` is destroyed. They live as long as the signal does, even if they will never be called, and can only get [garbage collected](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/0fd515bbb7070a502dd2fe6d16f5f3cbac591283/src/util/btcsignals.h#L240-L241) if new connections are added.

This behavior is different that previous boost signals behavior and causes a [deadlock](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/actions/runs/31848571315/job/94919834743) on GUI shutdown in #10102 because when the node registers signal callbacks (`handleInitMessage`, etc) that get forwarded to the GUI, the callbacks own `mp::EventLoopRef` references, and if the callbacks aren't freed, the node process can't shut down.

This change restores boost signals behavior freeing callbacks when they are disconnected or when `scoped_connection` objects are destroyed to avoid this problem and make callback lifetimes more predictable.

pulls.title: subprocess: fix command line memory leak on Windows
pulls.body:
`Popen::execute_process()` copied the command line into a buffer from `new[]`, but did not delete it. This leaked memory each time a process started on Windows.

`CreateProcessA` [needs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-createprocessa#:~:text=characters%2E-,The,violation) a writable command line buffer. Since C++17, `std::string::data()` supplies one, so give the `std::string` buffer directly and remove the copy.

This only affects Windows. It is only reachable if `-signer=<cmd>` is set, through authenticated RPC or the GUI. Each call leaks only the startup-defined `<cmd>`, and the rate is limited by process spawn time, so the impact is limited.

_edit: this was fixed upstream in https://github.com/arun11299/cpp-subprocess/pull/131, but since this codebase is C++20 it seems better to avoid the copy (and the const cast). A direct backport isn't possible anyway, since #35704 switched us to CreateProcessA._

pulls.title: interfaces: Avoid node crashes from invalid Chain IPC calls
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A program using the `Chain` IPC interface from #29409 can crash `bitcoin-node` with a single bad call: asking for a block hash above the tip, leaving the transaction argument of `broadcastTransaction` or `checkChainLimits` unset, or returning an error from a notification handler. Separately, `findAncestorByHash` reports success when the descendant block is unknown (#36472). The `Chain` methods were written for in-process C++ callers like the wallet, which follow documented preconditions, so they assert or dereference null instead of returning errors.

**Solution:** Make these `Chain` methods in `src/node/interfaces.cpp` return errors for invalid arguments, catch and log IPC errors from notification handlers, and fix the `findAncestorByHash` check. Three small commits, each with unit tests in `src/test/interfaces_tests.cpp`. Valid calls behave the same as before. Details are in the commit messages.

This PR does not depend on #29409, but the fixes matter if it is merged and `interfaces::Chain` is exposed over IPC. The problems were reported by zaidmstrr, willcl-ark and xyzconstant while reviewing #29409, and by enirox001 in #36472. The `findAncestorByHash` fix is the same one previously proposed by Romansage6 and Yudis-bit in #36473, #36484 and #36490.

pulls.title: Keep witness stacks in serialized form in CScriptWitness
pulls.body:
`CScriptWitness` stores a witness stack as a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`, which costs a 24-byte vector object and an allocation for every element. This makes it possible to construct transactions that take a large amount of memory after deserialization, while becoming very slow to deserialize.

This PR stores the stack as its serialization in a single allocation (or none if the stack is empty), with a small header holding its size and the offset of the last element. Witnesses can no longer be modified in place, only allowing replacing them entirely. Access to the individual witness stack elements is done by on-the-fly deserialization instead. `CScriptWitness` shrinks from 24 to 8 bytes, and `CTxIn` from 112 to 96 bytes.

The last commit also rejects transactions without inputs or outputs while deserializing P2P messages, as empty transactions would otherwise become the new worst case. Such messages are now ignored like other malformed messages. With it, the worst-case memory of a deserialized 4 MB block message drops from 112 MB to 24 MB.

Median deserialization time and memory of the deserialized block, master → PR:

| block | gcc (ms) | clang (ms) | memory (MB) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 4 MB: one witness with 2M 1-byte elements | 110.0 → 10.4 | 122.9 → 15.8 | 112 → 4.0 |
| 4 MB: one witness with 4M empty elements | 317.2 → 13.5 | 346.1 → 19.4 | 96 → 4.0 |
| 4 MB: empty transactions | 53.7 → 0.002 (rejected) | 55.4 → 0.002 (rejected) | 70 → none |
| 4 MB: transactions with 1 input and 1 output | 16.3 → 15.8 | 17.3 → 17.0 | 24.5 → 23.5 |
| 4M WU: 1 transaction, max inputs with 1-element witnesses | 1.96 → 2.37 | 2.21 → 2.61 | 3.5 → 3.1 |
| mainnet block 969729 | 2.44 → 2.54 | 2.58 → 2.70 | 3.6 → 3.0 |

So in addition to improving worst cases very significantly, it also provides modest memory usage improvements to the common case. This translates to mildly increasing the effective capacity of memory-bounded data structures that store transactions, like the mempool.

An alternative, or potential follow-up, is applying this approach to `CTransaction` as a whole rather than on a per-witness basis. Doing so would reduce the worst-case memory-per-weight for a transaction from 1.5 byte/WU (this PR) to 1.1 byte/WU (compared to ~28 byte/WU for master today).

Issue reported by furszy and 0xB10C.

pulls.title: addrman: use uniform sampling inside buckets
pulls.body:
The current way we sample from addresses within a bucket in addrman is randomized, but not perfectly random. It uses a linear scan, starting at a random position (out of the 64 positions in a bucket). This means that if for example only position 17 and 20 contain an address, 17 will be picked with probability 95.3% (whenever the initial position is 21..63 or 0..17) and 20 will be picked with probability 4.7% (whenever the initial position is 18..20).

Make this search perfectly uniform, regardless of distribution of addresses within the bucket, by first copying all non-empty positions to a temporary array, and then selecting uniformly randomly from that array.

Suggested by Crypt-iQ. Also pointed out earlier by mzumsande in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/23140#discussion_r733084509.

pulls.title: log: escape C1 control characters in messages
pulls.body:
The log escapes control characters so that a message cannot drive the terminal it is printed on, but it lets through the UTF-8 form of the C1 controls U+0080 to U+009F. VTE, the library behind GNOME Terminal and others, decodes these as CSI, OSC, DCS and the rest, like their `ESC [`, `ESC ]` and `ESC P` forms.

I escape the two-byte sequences 0xC2 0x80 to 0xC2 0x9F as `\xc2\x9b` and so on. Since 0xC2 is never a continuation byte, this needs no UTF-8 decoder, and all other non-ASCII text still passes untouched, as asked in #17095 and #35833. Single bytes 0x80 to 0x9F stay as they are, since they occur inside valid UTF-8. The new cases in `test_LogEscapeMessage` fail on master and pass with the change.

pulls.title: [RFC] Delayed transaction broadcast, minimal
pulls.body:
Note: planned to be reworked, see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36429#issuecomment-6315408546

Minimal implementation for "Delayed Transaction Broadcast" new feature.

Goal: Allow a user to submit a transaction for delayed broadcasting, that will be broadcast only later, at a randomized time. The aim is increased privacy, by making time-correlation-based tracking more difficult.
This fits together with private broadcast: private connection broadcast tries to hide the originator node; randomized delay tries to hide the creation time.

Goals in this PR: Extend the `sendrawtransaction` RPC with an optional `delay_for` parameter, and if set, postpone the initial broadcast to that later time, with some extra jitter.

Use case Details, with the limitations of the current changeset:
- What is a typical delay time? 30 - 90 minutes. (Too long times can get problematic: risk fee increase, node restart.)
- Delayed broadcast is only supported with private broadcast.
- Delay option and time is specified per submission (in `sendrawtransaction`). Alternative: with node level config.
- For now pending transactions are NOT persisted, so pending transactions will be lost during a node stop/restart/crash.
- Randomized delay is expressed as a percentage of the requested delay. A hard-coded value of 50% is used.
- Delay times are capped: requested delay between 0min to 12 hours, randomization range to minimum 5 minutes.
- Validation happens both at submission and broadcast time.
- No special handling for sudden fee increase situations.
- Pending (submitted but not yet broadcast) transactions can be inspected via existing `getprivatebroadcastinfo` RPC.
- The (pre-existing) `abortprivatebroadcast` RPC can be used to cancel a pending transaction submission.
- No special `nLockTime` handling, to be refined later.
- No special support from the wallet subsystem. (A submitted but not broadcast transactions is not visible in the wallet.)

Solution Details:
- The solution is based on the Private Broadcast implementation. 
- Transactions are stored in the already-existing `m_transactions` collection.
- A scheduled periodic check is added to check for transactions that have became due. The implementation is very similar to the existing retry logic (`ReattemptPrivateBroadcast`).
- Queue is not persisted currently, to be added later.

Related issue: #34118

pulls.title: test: make p2p_eviction actually exercise block-time protection
pulls.body:
`p2p_eviction.py` tests that 4 inbound peers that recently sent us a novel block are protected from eviction. However, the test currently passes even when that protection is not in effect. 

The block-sending peers are connected first, so they are the oldest connections. When block-time protection doesn't apply, `CompareNodeBlockTime` falls back to connection time and protects the 4 oldest peers, which are these same peers. Then the youngest remaining peer gets evicted. The check `evicted_peers[0] not in protected_peers` therefore holds whether or not block-time protection works.

This can be shown by deleting the line where the peers send their block (L71 on master):
```py
block_peer.send_blocks_and_test([block], node, success=True)
```

pulls.title: util, cli: name the Sock wait timeout cap and use it for -rpcclienttimeout=0
pulls.body:
Follow-up to #36340, addressing the review comments from pinheadmz and winterrdog there.

#36340 capped the `Sock::Wait`/`WaitMany` timeout at `INT_MAX` milliseconds (about 24.8 days) inside `WaitMany`. This moves that value to a named constant, `Sock::MAX_WAIT_TIMEOUT`, and mentions the cap in the doxygen comments of `Wait()` and `WaitMany()`, since it applies to every caller and not only to `bitcoin-cli`. The constant is a whole number of seconds (2147483 s), so `bitcoin-cli`, which works in seconds, uses exactly the same value as `Sock`.

`bitcoin-cli` still turned `-rpcclienttimeout=0` into a 5 year timeout. The timeout is applied to each wait for the socket, and each wait is now capped, so in practice `0` already means "give up after about 24.8 days without data". The 5 year value is replaced with `Sock::MAX_WAIT_TIMEOUT`, and the help text now says that 0 is the longest supported timeout (about 24 days) instead of no timeout.

There is no behaviour change. `sock_tests`, `interface_bitcoin_cli.py` (including the `-rpcclienttimeout=0` call added in #36340) and `interface_rpc.py` pass on macOS.

(Changes prepared with AI tools.)

pulls.title: mempool: remove time-based transaction expiry
pulls.body:
This is a simple mempool PR that fixes #33510.

Evicting mempool transactions by age (`-mempoolexpiry`, default two weeks) is
incentive-incompatible: it may drop transactions that could still be mined 
As discussed IRL and in #33510, this PR hence removes age-based eviction entirely.

Transactions now leave the mempool only via size limiting (`-maxmempool`),
replacement, conflicts, or inclusion in a block. The `EXPIRY` removal reason is
dropped. `-mempoolexpiry` is retained as a hidden no-op that warns when set, so
existing configurations keep starting.

Nice side effects:
- With expiry gone, the `entry_time` index has no readers. Removing it saves an
  ordered-tree node per mempool entry and drops a now unused Boost
  include.
- The `DynamicMemoryUsage()` per-entry estimate drops from three indexes to
  two, so within the same `-maxmempool` budget the mempool fits slightly more
  transactions.

pulls.title: span: diagnose dangling views from MakeByteSpan/MakeUCharSpan
pulls.body:
Follow-up to #36164, as suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36164#issuecomment-5541268260.

Tracked in https://github.com/kevkevinpal/bitcoin/issues/550.

**Problem:** `MakeByteSpan` and `MakeUCharSpan` return views into their input. A temporary container can leave those views dangling.

pulls.title: validation: check the most recent AssumeUTXO commitment during IBD
pulls.body:
**Problem:** AssumeUTXO verifies imported UTXOs against a hash we bake into the binary.
Every node reconstructs the same UTXO set during ordinary IBD, but [does not check its hash against the existing AssumeUTXO commitment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/32377).

**Fix:** During ordinary block validation, verify the provided AssumeUTXO hash when block connection reaches the corresponding block, stopping the node on a mismatch.
Flush pending changes to disk before hashing the UTXO set and comparing the result with the commitment.

Keep only the latest AssumeUTXO commitment per network to limit the extra hashing work during IBD, and update the release process to replace it.
Users who need older snapshots for research or other purposes can use a compatible older release or restore the corresponding commitment as `m_assumeutxo_data` and recompile.

pulls.title: RFC: Separate out runtime errors from BlockValidationState using `util::Expected`
pulls.body:
`BlockValidationState` currently carries two unrelated kinds of failure: consensus/policy invalidity which is the actual purpose and runtime errors via a `M_ERROR` mode in `ModeState` enum inside `ValidationState` class. This PR removes `M_ERROR` and routes runtime errors through `util::Expected<T, std::string>` instead, making the two failure modes distinct.

## Motivation

`BlockValidationState` exists to describe why a block or transaction is invalid. It holds a consensus/policy reject reason. A disk write or system runtime error is not that, yet it was folded into the same object as a third state i.e. `M_ERROR`.

This conflation has two costs:

- Wrong abstraction for non-validating functions. `FlushStateToDisk`, `DisconnectTip`, `ActivateBestChain`, `PreciousBlock`, and `InvalidateBlock` do no block validation, but each takes a `BlockValidationState` out-param to report any runtime error.

- Three outcomes in one object. Functions that can both validate and hit a runtime error (`ConnectBlock`, `AcceptBlock`, `ProcessNewBlock`) holds valid, invalid, and fatal into a single `BlockValidationState`, forcing every caller to unwrap.

As noted in the original discussion [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33856#discussion_r2765218331):

> Functions like FlushStateToDisk, ActivateBestChain aren't exactly about validating a certain block, yet they take a BlockValidationState& out-param just to absorb runtime errors, which feels like the wrong abstraction.

And also discussion [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35570#issuecomment-4783419874) to remove `M_ERROR` value.

- This would also pave a long term fix for #35570, which returns `BlockValidationState` from validation methods instead of boolean value.

`util::Expected` is a good option for this reason, it keeps the error handling in the same return value style (system/runtime errors and `ValidationState` for consensus correctness) and separates-out runtime errors from `ValidationState`.


Runtime errors could be signaled either by a return value or by throwing. This PR keeps them as return values as it's a minimal  change. `M_ERROR` was already a return-value mechanism  included in `ValidationState` with consensus verdict. This PR doesn't open the exceptions vs returns question, it keeps the existing return-value style and just moves the fatal error into a proper Expected channel.

pulls.title: net: serve `MSG_BLOCK` by stripping witnesses in place
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Serving blocks to legacy nodes currently decodes and reserializes them just to remove witnesses. `MSG_WITNESS_BLOCK` already avoids this work by serving the stored bytes directly. Faster witnessless IBD, as proposed in [#36476](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36476), also needs peers to serve these blocks efficiently.

**Fix:** Read disk-backed, non-Signet `MSG_BLOCK` replies into an owned byte buffer, check the header's proof of work and expected hash, and strip witness ranges from that buffer in place.

Extract a shared helper so decoding transactions and skipping their bytes follow the same encoding rules. Signet keeps `ReadBlock` for its solution check. Header checks now precede transaction parsing, so records corrupted in both places can log a different error.

**Performance:**

Time to read a block from disk and build its non-witness message:

| Block | Before | After | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `block413567` | 1.31 ms | 0.147 ms | **8.9x** |
| Same block with synthetic witnesses | 3.47 ms | 0.374 ms | **9.3x** |

The synthetic fixture adds a 512-byte witness item and an empty item to every input.

**Related work:** This extends the raw witness-block serving added in [#13151](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13151). The [#13011 discussion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13011#issuecomment-383145046) and the closed [#13098](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13098) identify unnecessary transaction hashing when serving historical blocks. The implementation also builds on the bulk block reads introduced in [#31551](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31551).

pulls.title: addrman: make `m_last_good` network-specific
pulls.body:
`m_last_good` is used to prevent recording failed attempts for addresses when it is our connectivity that is at fault.
However, it is quite common that only some networks are unreachable - e.g. I have encountered it frequently that `IPv6` is unreachable, while `IPv4` works fine. In this case it is not correct to increase the failed counter for an `IPv6` address  and ultimately making it `Terrible`, just because we are making `IPv4` connections.

Fix this by making `m_last_good` network-specific. 
Also change the initial value from 1 to 0, so that in a situation when there was no previous attempt for an address, but also no previous successful connection to its network, the failed count is not increased. The intial value was not a major issue previously because we would [only count failures](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/18c05d93016b28a9afd4c716dfe00b6e0accb30b/src/net.cpp#L2935-L2939) after having at least two outbound connections (in which case `m_last_good` would have been set).


pulls.title: [31.x] Backport #35168
pulls.body:
Backports:
* #35168

`v31.1` still has the pre-fix `LoadBlockIndex`. It re-adds a pruned block to `m_blocks_unlinked` when its parent is header-only (#35050). When the next block connects, `CheckBlockIndex` fails with `Assertion failed: (!foundInUnlinked)`. `-checkblockindex` is on by default only on regtest, so this crashes functional-test suites run against 31.x. pulls.title: guix: use `--load-path` for local modules
pulls.body:
Rather than exporting via `GUIX_PACKAGE_PATH`.

Fixes #36530.

pulls.title: ipc: hold event loop references when using it in `CapnpProtocol`
pulls.body:
`EventLoop::loop()` exits when its reference count reaches zero. In `serve()` mode, the parent connection is the only reference keeping the loop running. Other `CapnpProtocol` methods called from threads not handling parent IPC requests do not hold their own references and therefore depend on the parent connection remaining alive.

Add `loopRef()` (code suggested by @ryanofsky in https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/pull/376#discussion_r4268952676), which returns a new reference to the event loop or throws if the loop is not running or is shutting down, and use it in the methods that need the loop. Protect `m_loop` with a new `m_loop_mutex` to prevent `serve()` from destroying the loop while `loopRef()` is accessing it.

pulls.title: AssumeUTXO: allow retrying loadtxoutset after an interrupted load
pulls.body:
**Problem:** An interrupted `loadtxoutset` can leave an incomplete `chainstate_snapshot` database without its required `base_blockhash` marker. A later call can fail to open that database, requiring the operator to remove it manually before retrying.

**Fix:** Wipe the snapshot database before opening it so a later call can replace incomplete data. LevelDB acquires the database lock before deleting files, so a database held open by another load cannot be wiped. Also correct the startup warning to identify the missing marker and explain that retrying replaces the directory.

pulls.title: psbt: accept taproot ALL sigs with sighash unset
pulls.body:
SignPSBTInput() assumes SIGHASH_DEFAULT for a taproot input when
neither PSBT_IN_SIGHASH_TYPE nor the caller's sighash_type is set.
Its check of existing signatures then rejected every 65-byte
taproot signature, so a PSBT holding a valid SIGHASH_ALL signature
could be neither finalized nor signed further.

When neither the field nor the parameter is set, the default is only
assumed, so also accept a 65-byte signature ending in SIGHASH_ALL.
NONE, SINGLE and ANYONECANPAY variants are still rejected, as are
all mismatches when the field or the parameter is set.

Fixes #36507.

pulls.title: descriptor: speed-up `Parse` (xpub/xpriv) in ~30%
pulls.body:
This PR speeds up descriptor parsing, for basically descriptors that use xpub/xpriv, through some targeted improvements (I've been working on fuzz targets for wallet stuff for a while. I've noticed that some of them are slow so I started to work on understanding why and improve what can be improved. The finding came from it):

- Avoid redundant base58 decoding when parsing extended keys (this is the major improvement)

  ParsePubkeyInner unconditionally called both DecodeExtKey() and DecodeExtPubKey(), each running a full DecodeBase58Check (two SHA256 passes over ~111 bytes). A new DecodeExtKeyOrPubKey() function performs a single base58 decode and then checks the prefix, halving the cryptographic work per key. The interfaces of DecodeSecret, DecodeExtKey, and DecodeExtPubKey are also updated to accept string_view instead of const std::string&, eliminating unnecessary string copies in the descriptor parser and allowing DecodeBase58/DecodeBase58Check to use pointer-range iteration instead of strlen.

- Replace O(n) charset lookup with precomputed table

  DescriptorChecksum previously called std::string::find() for every character in the descriptor string, doing up to 96 comparisons per character. This replaces it with a 256-entry precomputed lookup table for O(1) lookups. The benefit scales with descriptor length.

pulls.title: wallet: fix migration of watch-only wallets with transactions
pulls.body:
Migrating a legacy wallet that holds no spendable material fails whenever the
wallet contains transactions. `migratewallet` returns
`std::bad_function_call (-1)` and the wallet is left unmigrated.

Two defects are involved, and the first one hides the second.

### 1. The migration check reads in-memory state that has not been updated yet

When the wallet being migrated has no spendable material,
`CWallet::ApplyMigrationData()` asserts that nothing is left behind in it:

```cpp
if (!m_address_book.empty()) return util::Error{_("Error: Not all address book records were migrated")};
if (!mapWallet.empty()) return util::Error{_("Error: Not all transaction records were migrated")};
```

The two checks look symmetric but are not. `DelAddressBookWithDB()` erases from
`m_address_book` straight away, so the first check sees current state.
`RemoveTxs()` only erases the transaction records from disk; it defers the
`mapWallet` removal to the db txn's `on_commit` listener, which does not run
until the txn is committed — after `ApplyMigrationData()` has returned.

`mapWallet` is therefore never empty at that point and the check always fails.

### 2. Aborting the txn calls a callback that was never set

`DbTxnListener` declares `on_commit` and `on_abort` as plain `std::function`
members and callers may set only the one they need. `RemoveTxs()` does exactly
that: `on_commit` is set, `on_abort` is left empty.

`TxnCommit()` and `TxnAbort()` each invoked their listener's callback
unconditionally, so the abort triggered by the failed check above threw
`std::bad_function_call`. The exception escaped the wallet entirely, replacing
the real error with an unhelpful one and skipping the caller's cleanup path.

### Fix

The first commit skips callbacks that are not set, and documents that they are
optional. The second discounts the transactions already queued for deletion
instead of requiring `mapWallet` to be empty.

They are kept separate because the second defect masks the first: with only the
listener fix applied, the migration surfaces the real error
`Error: Not all transaction records were migrated (-4)` instead of
`std::bad_function_call (-1)`.

### Testing

`src/wallet/test/db_tests.cpp` gains a regression test covering a listener with
only one callback set, for both commit and abort. It fails on master with
`std::bad_function_call` and passes with the fix.

`test/functional/wallet_migration.py` gains a case migrating a blank legacy
wallet with a watch-only address that has received a transaction. The test is
taken from #36483.

To reproduce on master, apply the functional test alone and run
`wallet_migration.py`.

Fixes #36483

pulls.title: net_processing: count presync work in chain sync eviction
pulls.body:
While our best header is below `-minimumchainwork`, a peer's headers first go through the PRESYNC phase of `HeadersSyncState`, and none of them are stored. So `pindexBestKnownBlock` stays null for the peer we're syncing from, and `ConsiderEviction` (net_processing.cpp:5504) treats it like an outbound peer that never announced a block:

1. it starts `CHAIN_SYNC_TIMEOUT` (20 min)
2. it sends a getheaders to "verify chain work"
3. after `HEADERS_RESPONSE_TIME` it disconnects with `Outbound peer has old chain, best known block = <none>`

This happens even though the peer is still sending headers. The presync progress is lost and the next peer starts from scratch.

On mainnet presync is roughly 480 headers round trips. If that takes more than ~22 minutes (about 2.5 s per round trip, e.g. over slow Tor or I2P), the sync peer gets evicted before presync can finish, and the same thing can happen with the next peer. The chain sync logic is from #11490, presync came later in #25717, and the two were never connected.

The timeout is not reset on presync work alone. When it is set, the work the peer has shown during presync is recorded, and when it expires the timeout is renewed for another `CHAIN_SYNC_TIMEOUT` only if that work has increased since. A peer that stops sending headers is therefore still asked once with getheaders and then disconnected, within about two periods (~42 minutes), as before. `m_headers_sync_mutex` is never held while taking `cs_main`, and `p2p_headers_sync_with_minchainwork.py` and `p2p_sendheaders.py` also pass with `DEBUG_LOCKORDER`.

The new `test_presync_peer_not_evicted` in `p2p_headers_sync_with_minchainwork.py` restarts a node with `-minimumchainwork=0x20000` (65536 headers). An outbound peer then sends it one full headers message per mocked minute for 25 minutes, so presync is still running at the end. On master the peer is disconnected after 24 minutes. With the fix it stays connected and `presynced_headers` keeps going up. `p2p_outbound_eviction.py`, `p2p_eviction.py` and `feature_minchainwork.py` still pass.

`test_presync_peer_stalled_is_evicted` covers the other side: a single outbound peer sends one headers message and then only answers pings, and it is disconnected after about 42 minutes of mocktime. That test fails without the progress check.

pulls.title: util: Clarify the assertion message in assertion failures (Assert, Assume, etc.)
pulls.body:
Clarify the message in case of assertion failures. Additionally unify the behavior of `NONFATAL_UNREACHABLE` w.r.t. abort handling.

Motivation: This was discussed in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34844#discussion_r3303436384

The error message generated by `Assert`, `Assume`, and `CHECK_NONFATAL` contains the failing assertion condition text, but it's unclear whether that's the failed expectation or the actual case. 

For example,
`"Internal bug detected: pindex != nullptr"`
in fact means that what happened was `pindex == nullptr`.

Clarify the situation, by inserting "\`%s\` check failed".

The above example is now:
``"Internal bug detected: `pindex != nullptr` check failed"``
which is more unambiguous.

Additionally, change `NONFATAL_UNREACHABLE` to behave like `CHECK_NONFATAL`, and honor the special abort setting (`G_ABORT_ON_FAILED_ASSUME`).

pulls.title: Encapsulation for CTransaction
pulls.body:
`CTransaction` currently exposes its data members publicly. This makes the implementation details of the type part of its interface.

This PR encapsulates the data members behind public observer functions. The existing users of `CTransaction` are migrated to the observers, after which the data members are made private.

The refactoring is deliberately split into three steps:

1. Add observer functions corresponding to the existing data members.
2. Migrate all users from direct data-member access to the observers.
3. Make the data members private.

The migration is automated with a new `bitcoin-tidy` `use-observers` check. This both makes the large mechanical change straightforward and provides a reusable tool for similar refactorings.

The split into separate commits allows reviewers to review handwritten changes independently of the automated changes. It also simplifies rebasing: if the mechanical migration conflicts, individual files can be reset to their new base versions and the migration tool can be run on them again. This works because the old interface remains available until the final commit, so the reset code is still valid while the mechanical migration is reapplied.

This PR does not change the semantics of `CTransaction`. In particular, regular value semantics are intentionally left for a subsequent change.

### Why Encapsulation? Why `CTransaction`?

Public data members make the representation of a type part of its API. Once access goes through observers, the representation can change without requiring its users to change as well. Potential changes are using shared immutable transaction state, or even an offset into shared immutable block state.

This establishes a clean boundary between the transaction's data and functionality that operates on it. In particular, it allows serialization/deserialization and other functionality to be separated from the data layout itself in subsequent refactorings.

This work is part of the broader interface-segregation direction described in #35904, but is not a prerequisite for the stateless validation library proposed there. The encapsulation has value independently of that work.

`CTransaction` is a good type to start this migration with: it is widely used, its interface is relatively simple, and its data members are already effectively immutable. This allows the migration to establish the pattern and tooling without first requiring changes to the semantics of the type.

pulls.body:
As there are ongoing changes to the Silent Payments public key extraction function `GetPubKeyFromInput` (see recently merged #36338, upcoming #36417), it seems reasonable to add benchmarks for it.
